<document>
<title>Rain of animals</title>
<fragment>
27. **^** "Fish rain takes Kerala villagers by surprise". *The Financial Express*. 14 February 2008.
28. **^** "Fish Rain", reported in the India : [2], October 24, 2009
29. **^** "It's raining fish in Northern Territory", reported in news.com.au : [3], February 28, 2010
30. **^** Lani Nami Buan (15 January 2012). "It's raining fish! It's normal". GMA News. Retrieved 16 January 2012.
31. **^** Jereco O. Paloma (15 January 2012). "Agusan's 'rain of fish' natural although unusual". SunStar Davao. Retrieved 16 January 2012.
32. **^** "Fish Rain", reported in the India : [4], September 12, 2013
33. **^** "Fish rain down on Sri Lanka village, reported in https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia : [5], 6 May 2014
34. **^** Archived August 14, 2015, at the Wayback Machine[*dead link*]
35. **^** Villagers wake up to find fish in fields!, *The Times of India*, August 17, 2015
36. **^** "Fish rain in diredawa Ethiopia.", http://mereja.com/news/1080799

</fragment>
<fragment>

After a reported rain of fish in Singapore in 1861, French naturalist Francis de Laporte de Castelnau speculated that a migration of walking catfish had taken place, dragging themselves over land from one puddle to another, following the rain.[7]


The likeliest explanation for many of the supposed cases is that there is no falling happening at all and the animals are driven along by winds or a deluge of some sort.[8] This explanation also accounts for the prevalence of reports that only a single species or type of animal is ever reported raining from the sky.


</fragment>
<fragment>
Reported meteorological phenomenon

File:Singapourfish.jpgA rain of fish was recorded in Singapore in 1861, when during three days of torrential rain numerous fish were found in puddles
![](image)Raining snakes, 1680.
A **rain of animals** is a rare meteorological phenomenon in which flightless animals fall from the sky. Such occurrences have been reported in many countries throughout history.[1] One hypothesis is that tornadic waterspouts sometimes pick up creatures such as fish or frogs, and carry them for up to several miles.[1][2] However, this aspect of the phenomenon has never been witnessed by scientists.[3]




## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Rain of flightless animals and things has been reported throughout history.[1] In the first century AD, Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder documented storms of frogs and fish.[4] In 1794, French soldiers saw toads fall from the sky during heavy rain at Lalain, near the French city of Lille.[5] Rural inhabitants in Yoro, Honduras claim "fish rain" happens there every summer, a phenomenon they call Lluvia de Peces.[6]



## Explanations

[edit]

![](image)Tornadoes and waterspouts may lift up animals into the air and deposit them miles away
French physicist André-Marie Ampère (1775–1836) was among the first scientists to take seriously accounts of raining animals. Addressing the Society of Natural Science, Ampère suggested that at times frogs and toads roam the countryside in large numbers, and that violent winds could pick them up and carry them great distances.[3]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Some cases are thought to be caused by birds dropping fish. With regard to a documented rain of fish that occurred on December 29, 2021 in Texarkana, Texas, independent researchers Sharon A. Hill and Paul Cropper proposed that the fish had been dropped or possibly regurgitated by passing birds.[20] The theory found some favor with airport workers who had cleaned up the fish; they noted that there were birds in the area around the same time, and the fish "were kind of chewed up". In June 2022 around the San Francisco coast, a boom of anchovies is likely to be the cause of fair weather falling of fish from birds' mouths, such as pelicans.[21]



## Occurrences

[edit]

The following list is a selection of examples.



### Fish

[edit]


</fragment>
</document>

<title>Religion in India</title>
<fragment>

A notable feature in religious ritual is the division between purity and pollution. Religious acts presuppose some degree of impurity, or defilement for the practitioner, which must be overcome or neutralized, before or during ritual procedures. Purification, usually with water, is thus a typical feature of most religious action.[133] Other characteristics include a belief in the efficacy of sacrifice and concept of merit, gained through the performance of charity or good works, that will accumulate over time and reduce sufferings in the next world.[133]


Muslims offer five daily prayers at specific times of the day, indicated by *adhan* (call to prayer) from the local mosques. Before offering prayers, they must ritually clean themselves by performing *wudu*, which involves washing parts of the body that are generally exposed to dirt or dust. A recent study by the Sachar Committee found that 3–4% of Muslim children study in *madrasas* (Islamic schools).[134]

<document>
<title>Religion in Australia</title>
<fragment>
The 2006 census[102] shows 53 listed groups down to 5000 members, most of them Christian denominations, many of them national versions such as Greek, Serbian Orthodox and Assyrian Orthodox. Of the smaller religions, Pagan religions 29,328, the Baháʼí Faith at 12,000, Humanism about 7000. Between 1000 and 5000 are: Taoism, Druse, Satanism, Zoroastrian, Rationalism, Creativity, Theosophy, Jainism. There are also adherents of Tenrikyo, Shinto, Unitarian Universalism, Eckankar, Cao Dai, Rastafari, Pantheism, Scientology and Raelianism.[103][104]


In general, non-Christian religions and those with no religion have been growing in proportion to the overall population.[105] With fewer classifications, data from 1996 and 2001 showed Aboriginal religion decreasing from 7000 to 5000 while Baháʼí grew from just under 9,000 to over 11,000 and the rest of the "Other" category growing from about 69,000 to about 92,000.[90]



### Paganism

[edit]

Main article: Paganism in Australia


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Religious affiliation in Australia, 1971-2021
"Over the past 50 years, there has been a steady decline in the proportion of Australians who reported an affiliation with Christianity. The same period has seen a consistent rise in Other religions and No religion, particularly in the last 20 years".[29]



### Total fertility rates

[edit]

As of 2016[update], Buddhists (1.68), Hindus (1.81) and the non-religious (1.84) had the lowest fertility rates. Christians (2.11) and Jews (2.17) had moderate fertility rates, and Muslims had the highest rate at 3.03.[30]



## Indigenous Australian traditions

[edit]

Main articles: Indigenous Australians, Australian Aboriginal mythology, and Dreaming (spirituality)


</fragment>
<fragment>
Religion in Australia, 2021 census[1][2]

1. Christianity (43.9%)
2. No religion (38.9%)
3. Unanswered (7.20%)
4. Islam (3.20%)
5. Hinduism (2.70%)
6. Buddhism (2.40%)
7. Sikhism (0.80%)
8. Other faiths (0.90%)

![](image)St Mary's Cathedral, Sydney


</fragment>
<fragment>

Other smaller groups also arrived and established their churches. Jews started arriving in the early 19th century. The Australian gold rushes brought in workers from China and the Pacific islands, as well as specialised workers from British India, such as the mainly Muslim "Afghan Cameleers".



### Indigenous Australian religion

[edit]

See also: Stolen Generations

![](image)Kolaia man wearing a headdress worn in a fire ceremony, Forrest River, Western Australia
Dreaming (spirituality) has been practised for tens of thousands of years. It is at once a collection of stories of an ancient view of creation and present day spirituality. It places significant emphasis on belonging to the land. It shaped and continues to shape Aboriginal law and customs; and Aboriginal art, story and dance continue to draw on these spiritual traditions.

<title>Religion in Australia</title>
<fragment>
The 2006 census[102] shows 53 listed groups down to 5000 members, most of them Christian denominations, many of them national versions such as Greek, Serbian Orthodox and Assyrian Orthodox. Of the smaller religions, Pagan religions 29,328, the Baháʼí Faith at 12,000, Humanism about 7000. Between 1000 and 5000 are: Taoism, Druse, Satanism, Zoroastrian, Rationalism, Creativity, Theosophy, Jainism. There are also adherents of Tenrikyo, Shinto, Unitarian Universalism, Eckankar, Cao Dai, Rastafari, Pantheism, Scientology and Raelianism.[103][104]


In general, non-Christian religions and those with no religion have been growing in proportion to the overall population.[105] With fewer classifications, data from 1996 and 2001 showed Aboriginal religion decreasing from 7000 to 5000 while Baháʼí grew from just under 9,000 to over 11,000 and the rest of the "Other" category growing from about 69,000 to about 92,000.[90]



### Paganism

[edit]

Main article: Paganism in Australia


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Religious affiliation in Australia, 1971-2021
"Over the past 50 years, there has been a steady decline in the proportion of Australians who reported an affiliation with Christianity. The same period has seen a consistent rise in Other religions and No religion, particularly in the last 20 years".[29]



### Total fertility rates

[edit]

As of 2016[update], Buddhists (1.68), Hindus (1.81) and the non-religious (1.84) had the lowest fertility rates. Christians (2.11) and Jews (2.17) had moderate fertility rates, and Muslims had the highest rate at 3.03.[30]



## Indigenous Australian traditions

[edit]

Main articles: Indigenous Australians, Australian Aboriginal mythology, and Dreaming (spirituality)


</fragment>
<fragment>
Religion in Australia, 2021 census[1][2]

1. Christianity (43.9%)

8. Other faiths (0.90%)

![](image)St Mary's Cathedral, Sydney


</fragment>
<fragment>

Other smaller groups also arrived and established their churches. Jews started arriving in the early 19th century. The Australian gold rushes brought in workers from China and the Pacific islands, as well as specialised workers from British India, such as the mainly Muslim "Afghan Cameleers".



### Indigenous Australian religion

[edit]

See also: Stolen Generations

![](image)Kolaia man wearing a headdress worn in a fire ceremony, Forrest River, Western Australia
Dreaming (spirituality) has been practised for tens of thousands of years. It is at once a collection of stories of an ancient view of creation and present day spirituality. It places significant emphasis on belonging to the land. It shaped and continues to shape Aboriginal law and customs; and Aboriginal art, story and dance continue to draw on these spiritual traditions.

<title>Religion in Honduras</title>
<fragment>
Religion in Honduras (Gallup CID 2022)[1]

1. Evangelicalism (44.0%)
2. Catholicism (36.0%)
3. Other (7.00%)
4. None (13.0%)

![](image)St. Rose's Cathedral in Santa Rosa de Copán
The predominant **religion in Honduras** is Christianity, representing 87% of the total population according to a 2017 estimate. The country is secular and the freedom of religion is enshrined in the nation's constitution.


The pre-Hispanic peoples that lived in actual Honduras were primarily polytheistic Maya and other native groups. In the 16th century, Roman Catholicism was introduced by the Spanish Empire and still holds a 46% share of the population. Protestantism accounts for 41% of the country's population.




## History

[edit]

### Ancient religion

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
### 20th century

[edit]

![](image)Cathedral of Saint Michael the Archangel
In recent years, the principal religious groups are Roman Catholic, Episcopal, Lutheran, Jehovah's Witness, Mennonite, approximately 300 evangelical Protestant groups, and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church) and well as communities of Muslims, Jews and Baha'is.[4]


The Catholic Church in Honduras is composed of eight dioceses: Tegucigalpa, Comayagua, Choluteca, Olancho, Yoro, San Pedro Sula, Trujillo and Copán which are a part of the Conference Episcopal of Honduras.


The Protestant churches are structured by three confederacies: The Pastors' Association of Honduras, the Evangelical Brotherhood of Honduras and the Apostolic Network of Honduras.


Both the Roman Catholic Church as well as the Protestant churches, especially the Pentecostal denominations, have experienced growth thanks in large part to modern forms of mass communication in recent decades.


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Mayan God Chaac in Copan sculpture museum
The Maya religion was the ancient one. It was practiced a lot in the timeline of the 4th and 7th century, AD. It was practiced in some parts of Central and South America, and it was based on polytheistic beliefs and had to do with a big number of rituals with occasional animals and maybe even human sacrifices. [*citation needed*]



### Post-colonial religion

[edit]

The second Roman Catholic Mass celebrated in the continental New World was on August 13, 1502, in Punta Caxinas, two weeks after the so-called "discovery" of Honduras by Christopher Columbus.[2][3] Thereafter, the Spanish began a process of converting and baptizing Honduran natives to the Catholic faith.


Honduras holds a small part of the former Mosquito Coast which came under British influence—now in the extreme southeast of the state. Protestant churches gained following in that sparsely populated area on the Caribbean coast, especially Anglicanism and the Moravian Church.




</fragment>
<fragment>

Foreign missionaries must register with the government. Some religious groups have reached agreements with the government to expedite this process;[4] however, some groups have noted difficulties in obtaining visas for longer than six months. 


Conscientious objection to military service is protected by law, including objection on religious grounds.[6]


Some politicians, generally from opposition parties, have regularly used antisemitism rhetoric in their political statements.[6][*dead link*]


In 2023, the country was scored 4 out of 4 for religious freedom according to Freedom House.[7]



## See also

[edit]

* Islam in Honduras
* Roman Catholicism in Honduras
* Virgin of Suyapa, perhaps Honduras' most popular religious image.
* Religion in Latin America
* ![flag](image) Honduras portal


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
</document>

![](image)Map of Sri Lanka, showing majority religions by D.S. Divisions, according to 2012 census.
Sri Lanka is officially a Buddhist country, while Sri Lankans practice a variety of religions. As of the 2012 census, 70.2% of Sri Lankans were Buddhists, 12.6% were Hindus, 9.7% were Muslims (mainly Sunni), 7.4% were Christians (mostly Catholics).[1][2] Buddhism is declared as the State religion of Sri Lanka and has been given special privileges in the Sri Lankan constitution such as the government is bound for protection and fostering of Buddhist Dharma throughout the nation.[3][4] However, the constitution also provides for freedom of religion and right to equality among all its citizens. In 2008 Sri Lanka was the third most religious country in the world according to a Gallup poll, with 99% of Sri Lankans saying religion is an important part of their daily life.[5]

The percentage of Christians has slowly declined from the height of 13% in 1891 they were 12.6% and numbered were 302,000. In 2012 they 7.4%. By the 1980s, the population of Christians was mostly concentrated in the northwest of Sri Lanka and in the capital where they are 10% of the population. Based on my research into documented cases of "raining fish" and the religious demographics of the countries where these phenomena have been reported, I can provide you with the following analysis:

## Countries with Documented Fish Rain Events and Their Predominant Religions:

**India** - Multiple documented cases (2008, 2009, 2013, 2015):
- Predominant religion: **Hinduism** (79.8%)
- Other significant: Islam (14.2%), Christianity (2.3%)

**Australia** - Northern Territory (2010):
- Predominant religion: **Christianity** (43.9%)
- "No religion" is the second largest group (38.9%)
- Other significant: Islam (3.2%), Hinduism (2.7%)

**Honduras** - Yoro (regular "Lluvia de Peces"):
- Predominant religion: **Christianity** (87% total)
- Breakdown: Evangelicalism (44%), Catholicism (36%)

**Sri Lanka** - Confirmed case (2014):
- Predominant religion: **Buddhism** (70.2%)
- Other significant: Hinduism (12.6%), Islam (9.7%), Christianity (7.4%)

**Ethiopia** - Dire Dawa case:
- Predominant religion: **Christianity** (Ethiopian Orthodox) and **Islam** (roughly split)

## Answer to Your Question:

**The predominant religion in countries experiencing fish rain is Christianity, but Hinduism dominates the single country with the most frequent documented cases - India.**

However, it's important to note that this phenomenon is **weather-related and not connected to religious beliefs or practices**. The distribution appears to correlate more with:

1. **Geographic and climatic conditions** conducive to waterspouts and tornadoes
2. **Population density and media coverage** (more likely to be reported in populated areas)
3. **Aquatic ecosystems** with abundant fish populations

India has the highest number of documented cases due to its large population, extensive coastline, and tropical climate conditions that favor such meteorological events, rather than any religious connection to Hinduism specifically.
